newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australia bank reforms seen as tidying-up effort.
newsitem.headline: Australia bank reforms seen as tidying-up effort.

text.p: Australia' latest financial reform proposals are aimed at tidying up existing rules and are unlikely to have the "Big Bang" effect of 1983's original deregulation, analysts said on Wednesday.

Australian Treasurer Peter Costello announced plans to loosen restrictions on mergers between banks and life offices, remove barriers to foreign takeovers of local banks and reform financial system regulation.
This was the main result of the Wallis Inquiry, named after its businessman-chairman Stan Wallis, was set up last June by Australia's conservative government to boost competition.

In 1983, the Campbell review of Australia's financial system led to the floating of the local dollar, the abolition of exchange controls, the end of lending restrictions and the entry of foreign banks into what had been a parcohial banking market.

"There were some major changes made post-Campbell Inquiry. It is difficult to see the things that come out of the Wallis Inquiry coming close to the same magnitude," said one economist, who declined to be named.
"...this one is tidying up a lot of loose ends such as prudential arrangements," said Peter Munckton, an economist at Bankers Trust.

The Wallis Inquiry, dubbed the 'Daughter of Campbell' recommended that a single agency oversee some financial regulatory operations and that the Reserve Bank of Australia remain responsible for the stabiliy of the bank system.

However, economists said they did not expect many of the recommendations to become law for some time. Costello said the government would announce further responses to the report after the May 13 federal budget.

"It could be 12 months before you see anything decent come out of this, except the six-pillars policy which is not law anyway -- it has always been at the discretion of the treasury," said Greg Matthews, equities manager at Mercantile Mutual.

The six pillars of Australia's financial institutions are the four major banks (Australia and New Zealand Banking Group Ltd, Commonwealth Bank of Australia, National Australian Bank Ltd and Westpac Banking Corp) plus the two major life insurance groups (Australian Mutual Provident Society and National Mutual Holdings Ltd).

The banking deregulation of the 1980s led to a credit binge with the newly-arrived foreign banks competing aggresively with the local banks for market share. This led huge bad debt write-offs in the early 1990s and the subsequent scaling-back of activities by many foreign banks.

The Wallis Inquiry recommendations are unlikely to create another lending binge as market conditions have changed with a lower-inflation environment now compared with the sharp asset price rises and high inflation of the late 1980s, analysts said.
The Wallis Inquiry said in its conclusion that despite the asset price boom of the late 1980s after deregulation, Australia's economy was in better shape because of it.

"The Inquiry concludes that Australia's economic structure in the 1990s is more competitive, more flexible and more capable of coping with the pressures of the current decade than would have been the case without financial deregulation," the Inquiry said in its 770-page report.
